sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: Horner syndrome, or oculosympathetic paresis, results from a lesion anywhere along the three-neuron sympathetic pathway supplying the eye and adnexa. It is classically characterized by the triad of miosis, partial ptosis, and facial anhidrosis. The severity of symptoms often depends on the chronicity and completeness of the sympathetic interruption.

branches: 1st Order (Central): Hypothalamus → Brainstem → Ciliospinal Center of Budge (C8-T2)
2nd Order (Preganglionic): C8-T2 → Over Lung Apex → Superior Cervical Ganglion (C2)
3rd Order (Postganglionic): SCG → Internal Carotid Artery → Cavernous Sinus → Orbit

sections.title: Classic Clinical Features
content: Miosis: Anisocoria is greater in dim light (failure to dilate).
Ptosis: 1-2mm due to paralysis of Müller’s muscle (Superior tarsal).
Inverse Ptosis: Elevation of the lower lid ('upside-down ptosis').
Dilation Lag: Sluggish pupillary redilation after light removal (pathognomonic).
Anhidrosis: Reduced sweating; location depends on lesion level.
Iris Heterochromia: Affected iris is lighter (if congenital/longstanding).

rows: Gliomas of the brainstem or spinal cord
CN III, IV, VI palsies often coexist

sections.title: Pharmacological Testing Protocol
content: Step 1: Confirm Horner with Apraclonidine 0.5% (Reversal of anisocoria) or Cocaine 4-10% (No dilation). Wait 30-45 mins.
Step 2: Allow 48-72 hours for washout before localization testing.
Step 3: Localize with Hydroxyamphetamine 1% (Paredrine). Dilation = 1st or 2nd Order; No Dilation = 3rd Order.
Step 4: Alternative Localization: Phenylephrine 1%. Dilation of Horner pupil only = 3rd Order (Denervation supersensitivity).

branches: 1st Order: Entire ipsilateral half of body
3rd Order: Absent or very localized (brow only)

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Immediate Emergency Workup
content: ACUTE PAINFUL HORNER: Suspect Internal Carotid Artery Dissection until proven otherwise.
Associated CN VI Palsy: Localization to the Cavernous Sinus (Parkinson’s Sign).
Hand Wasting / Weakness: Lower brachial plexus involvement (Klumpke's / Pancoast).
Thunderclap Headache: Possible SAH or vascular catastrophe.
New onset in Pediatrics: High risk for Neuroblastoma (Check urine VMA/HVA).

content.explanation: M: Mediastinum/Lung Apex (2nd Order). A: Artery/Carotid (3rd Order). P: Posterior Fossa/Brainstem (1st Order).

rows: Carotid Artery, Cavernous Sinus, Skull Base

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Neuroblastoma is the primary concern in non-traumatic pediatric Horner.
Workup includes MRI of entire sympathetic chain.
Urine catecholamines (VMA/HVA) have limited sensitivity but are part of the classic workup.
Congenital Horner often associated with birth trauma (brachial plexus injury).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The 'Harlequin' sign (unilateral facial flushing) may occur in first-order lesions.
Hydroxyamphetamine (Paredrine) testing is only valid if the 3rd order neuron is mature (wait >24 hours after injury).
Apraclonidine can produce a 'false negative' in acute cases (first 36-48 hours) before alpha-1 receptors upregulate.
In Horner syndrome, the anisocoria is most prominent in the first 5 seconds of darkness due to dilation lag.
